mcqs.q: The research process is defined as:
opts: A systematic sequence of scientific steps from problem to valid conclusions
The statistical analysis applied to the collected data
The procedure for obtaining ethical approval for a study
The writing and publication of a scientific paper
mcqs.explain: It is a structured, step-by-step approach used instead of guesswork, intuition or random actions.

mcqs.q: Which is NOT listed among the characteristics of the research process?
mcqs.explain: The process is explicitly a structured alternative to intuition and guesswork.

mcqs.q: In the overview of the research process, what immediately follows identifying the research problem?
mcqs.explain: The order is problem, literature review, research question, objectives and hypotheses, study design.

mcqs.q: A research problem is defined as:
opts: An unanswered question or gap in current knowledge
A statistical difficulty encountered during analysis
A failure to obtain ethical approval
A limitation in the available funding
mcqs.explain: Every research project begins with a problem.

mcqs.q: Which is NOT listed as a source of research problems?
opts: Clinical observations and daily medical practice
Published literature and public health priorities
mcqs.explain: Previous research recommendations are the seventh listed source.

mcqs.q: In the worked example, the observation that many obese patients develop hypertension becomes the research problem:
opts: Does obesity increase the risk of hypertension among adults?
What is the best treatment for hypertension?
mcqs.explain: The observation is converted into an unanswered question.

mcqs.q: In this lecture, a literature review is defined as:
opts: A systematic search and evaluation of existing scientific knowledge related to the research topic
A list of all references cited in the protocol
A summary of the results of the current study
The background section of a published paper
mcqs.explain: Its purposes are to determine what is known, identify gaps, avoid duplication, refine the question and select methodology.

mcqs.q: Which is NOT a stated purpose of the literature review?
opts: Obtain ethical approval for the study
Identify gaps in knowledge and avoid duplication
Refine the research question and select appropriate methodology
mcqs.explain: Ethical approval is a separate, later step.

mcqs.q: Google Scholar is listed as a literature source with the qualification that it should be used:
mcqs.explain: It indexes everything, including preprints, theses and predatory-journal content.

mcqs.q: Which is NOT listed among the tips for conducting a literature review?
opts: Limit the review to five key papers
mcqs.explain: Evaluating study quality is the fourth tip.

mcqs.q: A good research question should be all of the following EXCEPT:
mcqs.explain: Being too broad, for example asking what causes cancer, is listed as a common mistake.

mcqs.q: In the FINER criteria, the letter I stands for:
mcqs.explain: FINER is Feasible, Interesting, Novel, Ethical, Relevant.

mcqs.q: The FINER criteria are:
mcqs.explain: They are used to test the quality of a research question.

mcqs.q: In the PICO framework, C stands for:
mcqs.explain: PICO is Population/Patient, Intervention/Exposure, Comparison, Outcome.

mcqs.q: In the worked PICO example, home blood pressure monitoring is the:
mcqs.explain: The comparison is clinic-based monitoring and the outcome is improved blood pressure control.

mcqs.q: Which is a common mistake in formulating a research question?
opts: Vague wording such as “better” or “effective” without defining outcomes
Restricting the question to one population
mcqs.explain: Other mistakes include being too broad or too narrow and combining multiple questions into one.

mcqs.q: “High prevalence of hypertension” is an example of a:
mcqs.explain: The research problem is the broad issue requiring investigation.

mcqs.q: “To investigate the relationship between obesity and hypertension” is an example of a:
mcqs.explain: The aim is the overall purpose; the objectives are the specific measurable goals.

mcqs.q: Objectives are best described as:
opts: Specific measurable goals stating what the study intends to accomplish
A testable prediction of the result
The blueprint for answering the question
mcqs.explain: The general objective gives the broad purpose and the specific objectives give concrete, measurable aims.

mcqs.q: A hypothesis is:
opts: The overall purpose of the study
The method used to collect data
mcqs.explain: It is stated as a null hypothesis and an alternative hypothesis.

mcqs.q: “There is no association between obesity and hypertension” is the:
mcqs.explain: The alternative hypothesis states that obesity is associated with hypertension.

mcqs.q: The study design is best described as:
opts: The blueprint for answering the research question
The statistical test applied to the data
The plan for obtaining ethical approval
The structure of the final report
mcqs.explain: It is chosen at step 5, after the objectives and hypotheses are set.

mcqs.q: Which is an OBSERVATIONAL study design?
mcqs.explain: The observational designs listed are cross-sectional, case-control and cohort; the experimental ones are the RCT and the quasi-experimental study.

mcqs.q: Choosing a study design depends on all the following EXCEPT:
opts: The citation count of previous studies
mcqs.explain: The five listed determinants are the research question, ethics, resources, time and disease frequency.

mcqs.q: A research protocol is:
opts: The detailed plan for conducting the study
The application form submitted to the journal
The consent form signed by participants
The final report of the results
mcqs.explain: A well-written protocol ensures consistency and reproducibility.

mcqs.q: Which is NOT listed among the typical components of a research protocol?
opts: Statistical analysis plan and ethical considerations
mcqs.explain: The sixteen components run from the title through to the references.

mcqs.q: Before recruiting participants, the researcher must:
opts: Submit the protocol to the IRB or Ethics Committee and obtain approval before data collection
Register the study with a journal
mcqs.explain: No participant contact or data collection may occur before approval.

mcqs.q: Which is NOT one of the four ethical principles listed in this lecture?
mcqs.explain: Reproducibility is a characteristic of the research process, not one of the four ethical principles.

mcqs.q: In informed consent, participants should understand:
opts: Purpose, procedures, risks, benefits, confidentiality and the right to withdraw
Only the purpose and the benefits
Only the risks and the researcher's name
Only the funding source of the study
mcqs.explain: Consent is obtained after IRB approval and before data collection.

mcqs.q: Which is NOT listed among the data sources for data collection?
mcqs.explain: Published reviews belong to the literature review, not to primary data collection.

mcqs.q: During data collection the researcher must ensure:
opts: Standardized procedures, trained data collectors, accurate documentation and confidentiality
The largest possible sample regardless of the protocol
That all participants are known to the research team
mcqs.explain: Data are collected according to the protocol.

mcqs.q: The first tasks after data collection are to:
opts: Clean the data, code variables, and enter data into statistical software
Submit the paper to a journal
mcqs.explain: Descriptive analysis is then performed, followed by inferential analysis if appropriate.

mcqs.q: Which is an example of DESCRIPTIVE analysis?
opts: Mean, median, standard deviation, frequency and percentages
mcqs.explain: Chi-square, t-test, ANOVA, correlation and regression are inferential analyses.

mcqs.q: Which is an example of INFERENTIAL analysis?
mcqs.explain: Inferential analyses listed are chi-square, t-test, ANOVA, correlation and regression.

mcqs.q: Which is NOT listed among the common statistical software packages?
mcqs.explain: The five listed are SPSS, R, Stata, SAS and Jamovi.

mcqs.q: Findings should be interpreted in relation to:
opts: Objectives, hypothesis, existing literature and clinical relevance
mcqs.explain: Interpretation precedes reporting and dissemination.

mcqs.q: In the IMRAD structure, the letters stand for:
mcqs.explain: It is the standard structure of a research report.

mcqs.q: Which is NOT listed as a channel of dissemination?
mcqs.explain: Publishing allows findings to contribute to evidence-based practice.

mcqs.q: Bias and confounding are classified as:
mcqs.explain: The scientific challenges are a poor research question, inappropriate design, small sample size, bias, confounding and missing data.

mcqs.q: Difficulty recruiting participants and equipment limitations are:
mcqs.explain: Limited funding and time constraints are the other practical challenges.

mcqs.q: Confidentiality breaches, inadequate informed consent and conflicts of interest are:
mcqs.explain: They arise throughout the research process, not only at the approval stage.

saqs.q: Define the research process and list its characteristics and sequential steps.
saqs.a: THE RESEARCH PROCESS — a systematic sequence of scientific steps used to identify a problem, collect and analyze data, and generate valid conclusions; a structured step-by-step approach instead of guesswork or intuition. CHARACTERISTICS — systematic, logical, objective, ethical, reproducible, evidence-based. STEPS — identify the problem · literature review · develop the question · objectives and hypotheses · study design · protocol · ethical approval · data collection · analysis · interpretation · report writing · publication and dissemination.

ans.text: A systematic sequence of scientific steps used to identify a problem, collect and analyze data, and generate valid conclusions — a structured, step-by-step approach instead of guesswork, intuition or random actions.

saqs.q: Explain how a research problem is identified and list the sources of research problems.
saqs.a: A research problem is an unanswered question or gap in current knowledge. SOURCES — clinical observations, daily medical practice, published literature, public health priorities, hospital records, patient concerns, previous research recommendations. EXAMPLE — the observation that many obese patients develop hypertension becomes: does obesity increase the risk of hypertension among adults?

ans.text: Every project begins with a problem — an unanswered question or gap in current knowledge.
Example — the observation that many obese patients develop hypertension becomes the research problem: does obesity increase the risk of hypertension among adults?

saqs.q: Describe the purposes, sources and practical tips of the literature review in the research process.
saqs.a: A systematic search and evaluation of existing knowledge on the topic. PURPOSES — determine what is known, identify gaps, avoid duplication, refine the question, select methodology. SOURCES — PubMed, Scopus, Web of Science, Cochrane Library, Google Scholar with critical appraisal, university library databases. TIPS — use recent studies, prefer peer-reviewed journals, evaluate study quality, keep accurate references.

ans.text: A systematic search and evaluation of existing scientific knowledge related to the research topic.

saqs.q: Explain how to formulate a research question, including the FINER and PICO frameworks and the common mistakes.
saqs.a: A good question is clear, focused, feasible, relevant, ethical and novel. FINER — Feasible, Interesting, Novel, Ethical, Relevant. PICO — Population, Intervention/Exposure, Comparison, Outcome; e.g. in adults with hypertension, does home BP monitoring compared with clinic-based monitoring improve BP control? MISTAKES — too broad; too narrow; vague wording ('better', 'effective') without defined outcomes; multiple questions combined; unanswerable ethically or scientifically; lacking clinical or public health relevance; ignoring existing evidence and duplicating established findings.

ans.text: A good research question is clear, focused, feasible, relevant, ethical and novel.
Example — in adults with hypertension, does home blood pressure monitoring, compared with clinic-based monitoring, improve blood pressure control?

list: Ignoring existing evidence and duplicating well-established findings without justification

saqs.q: Distinguish between the research problem, research question, aim and objectives, and explain the null and alternative hypotheses.
saqs.a: PROBLEM — the broad issue (high prevalence of hypertension). QUESTION — the specific question (is obesity associated with hypertension among adults?). AIM — the overall purpose (to investigate the relationship). OBJECTIVES — specific measurable goals; GENERAL (broad purpose) and SPECIFIC (concrete measurable aims). HYPOTHESIS — a testable prediction: NULL states no association between obesity and hypertension; ALTERNATIVE states obesity is associated with hypertension.

saqs.q: List the components of a research protocol and state what is done at the ethical approval step.
saqs.a: PROTOCOL — the detailed plan: title, background, research question, objectives, hypothesis, methodology, study design, study population, sampling method, sample size, data collection tools, statistical analysis plan, ethical considerations, timeline, budget, references; it ensures consistency and reproducibility. ETHICAL APPROVAL — before recruiting, submit the protocol to the IRB or Ethics Committee and obtain approval before data collection. PRINCIPLES — respect for persons, beneficence, non-maleficence, justice. CONSENT requires understanding purpose, procedures, risks, benefits, confidentiality and the right to withdraw.

list: Title · background · research question · objectives · hypothesis
Methodology · study design · study population · sampling method · sample size

ans.text: A well-written protocol ensures consistency and reproducibility.

At the ethical approval step — before recruiting participants, submit the protocol to the IRB or Ethics Committee and obtain approval before data collection. The principles are respect for persons, beneficence, non-maleficence and justice, and informed consent requires that participants understand the purpose, procedures, risks and benefits, as well as confidentiality and the right to withdraw.

saqs.q: Describe data collection, data analysis, interpretation and dissemination in the research process.
saqs.a: COLLECTION — per protocol, from questionnaires, interviews, medical records, examination, laboratory tests, imaging and EHRs; ensure standardized procedures, trained collectors, accurate documentation and confidentiality. ANALYSIS — clean data, code variables, enter into software (SPSS, R, Stata, SAS, Jamovi); descriptive first (mean, median, SD, frequency, percentage), then inferential (chi-square, t-test, ANOVA, correlation, regression). INTERPRETATION — against objectives, hypothesis, literature and clinical relevance, reported in IMRAD. DISSEMINATION — journals, conferences, posters, institutional reports, clinical guidelines.

saqs.q: List the common challenges in the research process under their three headings.
saqs.a: SCIENTIFIC — a poor research question, inappropriate study design, small sample size, bias, confounding, missing data. PRACTICAL — limited funding, time constraints, difficulty recruiting participants, equipment limitations. ETHICAL — confidentiality breaches, inadequate informed consent, conflicts of interest.
